action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal putamina without atrophy, hyperintense rim or hypointensity; normal midbrain, pons and cerebellar peduncles; mild age-appropriate atrophy with Fazekas 1 change; no infarct or hydrocephalus
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm 72/min with ventricular pre-excitation (PR 100 ms, delta waves, QRS 120 ms); no acute ST change
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG for the two syncopal episodes in a patient with known WPW
action_criteria.rationale: Every syncope needs a 12-lead ECG; here it documents whether the pre-excitation persists before the syncope is attributed to an orthostatic or an arrhythmic mechanism [ESC_2018]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Persistent pre-excitation without SVT, atrial fibrillation or pauses; both symptomatic light-headedness events in sinus rhythm at 76 and 78/min
action_criteria.label: 24-hour Holter to correlate symptoms with rhythm in known pre-excitation
action_criteria.rationale: The syncopes were attributed to WPW without a documented arrhythmia; rhythm-symptom correlation during his light-headed spells on standing tests that attribution [ESC_2018]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal left ventricular size and function, EF 61%, no valve disease, hypertrophy or Ebstein anomaly
action_criteria.label: Consider a transthoracic echocardiogram to exclude structural heart disease associated with pre-excitation
action_criteria.rationale: Pre-excitation can accompany structural heart disease (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Ebstein anomaly), which would change the syncope risk; the ECG and Holter carry the main question [ESC_2018]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reduced cardiac MIBG uptake (early H/M 1.48, delayed H/M 1.26, washout 34%): cardiac sympathetic denervation
action_criteria.label: Consider cardiac MIBG scintigraphy if the PD versus MSA question remains after examination and MRI
action_criteria.rationale: Early orthostatic hypotension raises MSA; postganglionic cardiac denervation is usual in PD and uncommon in MSA, although the rest tremor, validated olfactory loss and normal MRI already favour PD [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Slowed processing speed (PSI 82, Trail Making A 42 s, B 118 s), reduced fluency, verbal learning and visual delayed recall, with normal naming and figure copy; GDS 8/15, BAI 12
action_criteria.label: Consider a neuropsychological battery to characterise the cognitive impairment (MoCA 24/30)
action_criteria.rationale: Difficulty multitasking contributed to his early retirement and the MoCA is 24/30; a battery characterises the PD mild cognitive impairment at level II and screens mood [Litvan_2012]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Tamsulosin and amlodipine identified as contributors to the orthostatic fall that levodopa may deepen; clonazepam identified as a sedation and fall risk
action_criteria.label: Review the medication list for drugs that worsen orthostatic hypotension and falls before starting levodopa
action_criteria.rationale: He has measured orthostatic hypotension with syncope while taking tamsulosin and amlodipine, and takes clonazepam; drug review is part of the treatment of orthostatic syncope [ESC_2018]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a patient with cognitive impairment
Do not label the syncope arrhythmic on the strength of the pre-excitation pattern alone, without an arrhythmia documented during symptoms
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015) with PD mild cognitive impairment: left-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, rigidity and a left-hand rest tremor; one red flag (orthostatic fall of 32/20 mmHg at 3 minutes within 5 years of onset) counterbalanced by two supportive criteria (rest tremor, and olfactory loss on Sniffin' Sticks 6/12); MoCA 24/30 without loss of independence (MDS level I) [Postuma_2015][Litvan_2012]

Attribute both syncopes to orthostatic hypotension rather than to WPW: both occurred on standing, the measured fall of 32/20 mmHg with a heart-rate rise of only 6/min is neurogenic in pattern, and both symptomatic Holter events were in sinus rhythm; ask cardiology to risk-stratify the accessory pathway separately, without attributing the syncope to it [ESC_2018]

Treat the orthostatic hypotension: review and where possible stop tamsulosin and amlodipine, advise 2 to 2.5 L of fluid a day, slow staged rising, head-up tilt of the bed and abdominal compression; if symptoms persist, consider midodrine or fludrocortisone with supine blood pressure monitoring [ESC_2018]

Start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), review the response after 2 to 3 months, and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each step; prefer levodopa to a dopamine agonist, which worsens orthostatic hypotension and adds hallucination and sleepiness risk [NICE_NG71]
Keep the bedroom safety measures for the REM sleep behaviour disorder and review clonazepam, which adds sedation and fall risk with orthostatic hypotension; melatonin is an alternative

avoided_actions.rationale: Both episodes occurred on standing with prompt recovery and no features of a seizure: EEG is not indicated in syncope
No infectious, inflammatory or rapidly progressive feature: CSF has no role in this parkinsonism
A DaTscan does not separate PD from MSA or PSP [Marshall_2009]
Formal autonomic testing is not part of the PD work-up; bedside orthostatic blood pressure already documents the neurogenic orthostatic hypotension

Pre-excitation persists on ECG and Holter, but both syncopes occurred on standing, the orthostatic fall is neurogenic in pattern and both symptomatic Holter events were in sinus rhythm
Coexists: both drugs lower standing pressure and contribute, but a 32/20 mmHg fall with a heart-rate rise of 6/min indicates a neurogenic component; not the cause of the parkinsonism

key_clinical_evidence: Left-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and an intermittent 4-5 Hz left-hand rest tremor: parkinsonism with one supportive criterion on examination [Postuma_2015]
Olfactory loss on Sniffin' Sticks (6/12): a validated olfactory test, the second supportive criterion [Postuma_2015]

Orthostatic fall of 26/16 mmHg at 1 minute and 32/20 mmHg at 3 minutes with a heart-rate rise of 6/min: neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, one MDS red flag, with tamsulosin and amlodipine as contributors
Both syncopes occurred on standing; the Holter shows persistent pre-excitation with symptomatic events in sinus rhythm: orthostatic, not arrhythmic, syncope [ESC_2018]
PSG-confirmed REM sleep behaviour disorder for 3 years, constipation for 3 years and erectile dysfunction before the motor signs: prodromal synucleinopathy features [Berg_2015]

contraindications: Non-selective MAO inhibitors with levodopa: risk of hypertensive crisis.
interactions: Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker) lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Amlodipine lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further.
Clonazepam adds sedation and fall risk with dopaminergic drugs in older patients.
warnings: Midodrine can be considered for symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; it raises supine blood pressure (measure it lying, avoid doses within 4 hours of bedtime) and can cause reflex bradycardia.
Fludrocortisone causes fluid retention, hypokalaemia and supine hypertension.
Omeprazole and polyethylene glycol 3350: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle due to the co-existing WPW syndrome serving as a major red herring for syncope etiology. The known pre-excitation plausibly explains the syncopal episodes, potentially diverting the agent from the orthostatic mechanism and the broader constellation of prodromal alpha-synucleinopathy features. The early neurogenic orthostatic hypotension also raises MSA-P, which the asymmetric rest tremor, validated olfactory loss and normal MRI argue against.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Daniel Kowalczyk is a 62-year-old right-handed retired electrical engineer who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of recurrent syncopal episodes, progressive motor slowing, and gait instability that have evolved over the past eighteen months. His medical history is notable for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome diagnosed at age 42 after a witnessed syncopal episode with documented delta waves on ECG, which was managed conservatively as he remained asymptomatic for over fifteen years. Eight months ago, he experienced a syncopal episode while standing in his garage workshop, falling backward and striking his occiput on a workbench. He was evaluated in the emergency department, and the event was attributed to a possible re-entrant tachycardia because of his known WPW. A second syncopal episode occurred four months later while standing from a seated position at a restaurant, and was similarly attributed to his WPW by his cardiologist. However, his wife has become increasingly concerned about changes beyond the syncope. She reports that over the past eighteen months, his movements have become noticeably slower and more deliberate. He now takes considerably longer to dress in the morning, struggles with buttons and zippers, and his handwriting has become progressively smaller and harder to read. His walking pace has diminished markedly, and she has noticed that he no longer swings his left arm naturally when walking. Over the past six months she has also seen an intermittent tremor of his left hand while it rests on the armrest. He has had three near-falls, two of them when light-headed after standing up, though he has managed to catch himself or grab nearby support. His chronic constipation, present for approximately three years, has worsened significantly despite daily polyethylene glycol, and he sometimes goes four to five days without a bowel movement. He has nocturia once or twice a night, unchanged since tamsulosin was started for his prostate, and denies urinary urgency or incontinence. His erectile dysfunction preceded the motor symptoms by approximately six months. Three years ago, his wife began sleeping in a separate bedroom because he was thrashing, kicking, and shouting during sleep, sometimes enacting what appeared to be fighting or running in his dreams. A sleep study confirmed REM sleep behavior disorder. He reports mild difficulty with multitasking at work, which contributed to his early retirement six months ago. He has noticed he cannot smell his morning coffee anymore and initially attributed this to aging. He denies visual hallucinations. He has not been exposed to neuroleptics, metoclopramide, or other dopamine-blocking agents. The referring cardiologist has been focused on the WPW syndrome as the explanation for his syncopal episodes, but his wife specifically requested a neurology referral because she feels the motor and balance changes are a separate and worsening problem.

neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing intact. Rapid alternating movements are slow, more on the left, without cerebellar-type irregularity or decomposition.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. No vertical gaze palsy. Facial expression mildly hypomimic bilaterally. Decreased blink rate noted. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Mild decreased olfaction reported by patient (unable to identify coffee grounds during bedside testing).
neurological_exam.gait: Narrow-based. Reduced arm swing, more on the left. Stride length mildly shortened. Turns require 4-5 steps. Pull test: two steps backward with unaided recovery. No festination. No freezing of gait.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, date, and situation. MMSE 27/30 (lost 1 point on serial sevens, 1 point on delayed recall, 1 point on pentagon copy). MoCA 24/30, losing one point each on trail-making, clock drawing (numbers correctly placed but hands slightly mispositioned), serial subtraction and letter fluency, and two on delayed recall. Speech is mildly hypophonic. Affect somewhat flat but appropriate. No confabulation or perseveration.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, more prominent on the left than the right. Mild axial rigidity. Bradykinesia with progressive decrement in amplitude and speed on finger tapping, hand opening and closing and pronation-supination, clearly worse on the left and mild on the right. Intermittent low-amplitude 4-5 Hz rest tremor of the left hand, brought out by mental distraction and suppressed by voluntary movement. No pronator drift. No myoclonus or dystonia.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, and patellar bilaterally. Achilles reflexes 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No palmomental or grasp reflex.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally. Vibration sense mildly reduced at ankles bilaterally. Romberg negative.
